summary: An informational memo describing the "advanced" parts of the sockets programming interface that applications need to use extra IPv6 features, beyond the basic API. It gives programmers a common way to reach those features across systems. It was replaced by RFC 3542.

plainLanguage.summary: Programs talk through a socket like a phone. This memo adds extra buttons to the phone so programs can use the special tricks of the newer internet addressing system.

questions: how do programs use extra ipv6 features
how do programs use ipv6 raw sockets
how do programs specify which interface to send on
subtitle: API extensions for programs to access raw sockets and IPv6 extension headers.

tldr.problem: The basic IPv6 sockets API covers TCP and UDP applications, but advanced programs like Ping, Traceroute, routing daemons, and multicast routers need access to raw sockets, extension headers, and per-packet information that the basic API does not provide.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2292 defines structures and functions for IPv6 raw sockets (ICMPv6, IGMPv6, and custom protocols), access to IPv6 extension headers (Hop-by-Hop options, Destination options, Routing header), packet information (interface, addresses, hop limit), and ancillary data macros for passing this information with regular send and receive calls.
tldr.outcome: Programs can now portably access IPv6 advanced features across different operating systems without each vendor reimplementing raw socket handling differently. RFC 2292 was later replaced by RFC 3542.

today: RFC 2292 is an Informational document describing the Advanced Sockets API for IPv6. It was later refined and obsoleted by RFC 3542 in May 2006, which updated the API with additional features and clarifications.

sections.title: Why Advanced IPv6 Programs Need New APIs
sections.content:
The basic IPv6 sockets API (defined elsewhere) works well for TCP and UDP applications: web browsers, mail clients, file transfer, telnet, and similar client-server programs. But another class of programs exists that needs deeper access to the network: Ping, Traceroute, routing daemons (OSPF for IPv6, RSVP), multicast routing daemons, router discovery daemons, and neighbor discovery daemons.

These programs need features the basic API does not provide: raw sockets to send and receive ICMPv6 (the Internet Control Message Protocol for IPv6), IGMPv6 (Internet Group Management Protocol for IPv6), and arbitrary protocols; the ability to specify and read IPv6 extension headers (Hop-by-Hop options, Destination options, and source routing); and the ability to determine which interface a packet arrived on, to specify the outgoing interface, and to control the hop limit on a per-packet basis.

Unlike IPv4, where most implementations started from common Berkeley source code, IPv6 had no common base, making portability hard without standardization. This RFC provides that standardization.
sections.plainLanguage: Most programs just send and receive messages like a telephone. But some programs (like network doctors) need to look at the raw packets and the headers to debug the network.

sections.title: IPv6 Headers and Constants
sections.content:
The ip6_hdr structure defines the IPv6 header fields: version (4 bits), traffic class / priority (8 bits), flow label (20 bits), payload length, next header type, and hop limit, followed by 128-bit source and destination addresses.

The next header field is numeric and identifies which type of data follows the IPv6 header: 0 for Hop-by-Hop options, 6 for TCP, 17 for UDP, 41 for tunneled IPv6, 43 for Routing header, 44 for Fragment header, 50 for Encapsulating Security Payload, 51 for Authentication header, 58 for ICMPv6, 59 for no next header, and 60 for Destination options.

Extension headers follow a common format with a next-header field and length field (in 8-octet units), followed by type-specific data. The RFC defines structures for all extension headers except Authentication and Encryption.

ICMPv6 header includes type, code, checksum, and type-specific fields. Common types include Echo Request (128), Echo Reply (129), Router Solicitation (133), Router Advertisement (134), Neighbor Solicitation (135), Neighbor Advertisement (136), and Redirect (137).
sections.plainLanguage: IPv6 headers have many fields describing the packet: where it came from, where it is going, what type of data it is, and how many hops it can make.

sections.title: Raw Sockets and ICMP
sections.content:
Raw sockets allow applications to send and receive datagrams with arbitrary protocols. With IPv4, applications could create raw ICMPv4, IGMPv4, or custom-protocol sockets; with IPv6, raw sockets are used for ICMPv6, custom-protocol sockets, and routing protocols like OSPF (IPv6 protocol 89) or RSVP (protocol 46).

All data sent via raw IPv6 sockets must be in network byte order (big-endian); received data is also in network byte order. This differs from IPv4 raw sockets, which were ambiguous about byte ordering.

When the kernel processes an ICMPv6 raw socket, it automatically calculates and stores the ICMPv6 checksum (which is mandatory for ICMPv6). For other raw IPv6 sockets, the application must use the IPV6_CHECKSUM socket option to have the kernel compute and verify checksums, specifying the offset into the user data where the checksum belongs. This prevents applications from having to manually select source addresses for checksum calculation.

ICMPv6 raw sockets can receive many message types: error messages (unreachable, packet-too-big, time-exceeded, parameter-problem), informational messages (echo-request, echo-reply), and neighbor discovery messages (router-solicit, router-advert, neighbor-solicit, neighbor-advert, redirect). Most applications only care about a few types, so the API provides an icmp6_filter structure and macros (ICMP6_FILTER_SETPASS, ICMP6_FILTER_SETBLOCK, and others) to allow applications to filter by message type, reducing kernel-to-application traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: Raw sockets let programs send and receive the low-level network packets that normal applications never see. The kernel helps by calculating checksums and filtering out messages the program does not care about.

sections.title: Ancillary Data and Packet Information
sections.content:
The msghdr structure (used by sendmsg() and recvmsg() functions) has two fields for "ancillary data": msg_control (a pointer) and msg_controllen (a length). Ancillary data is how applications and the kernel pass extra information alongside the main message data.

Each ancillary data object is preceded by a cmsghdr structure containing the object's length, originating protocol level, and type. The RFC defines five macros for working with ancillary data: CMSG_FIRSTHDR() (get pointer to first object), CMSG_NXTHDR() (get next object), CMSG_DATA() (get data within an object), CMSG_SPACE() (space needed for an object including padding), and CMSG_LEN() (length of an object's header plus data).

Using ancillary data, applications can specify and receive the following per-packet information: the interface on which a packet arrived (or will be sent), the source and destination addresses, the hop limit, and (advanced) the next-hop address. Applications can also send and receive IPv6 extension headers (Hop-by-Hop options, Destination options, and Routing header) as ancillary data rather than as part of the main packet buffer, making it easier to parse and construct complex headers.
sections.plainLanguage: Ancillary data is like a special pocket on an envelope where you can attach extra information (the interface, the hop limit) that travels with the main message.

sections.title: Extension Headers: Options and Routing
sections.content:
Hop-by-Hop options are processed by every node along a packet's path. Applications send and receive them as ancillary data using IPV6_HOPOPTS. The RFC provides helper functions like inet6_option_space() (allocate space), inet6_option_init() (initialize), inet6_option_append() (add an option), and inet6_option_find() (search for an option type).

Destination options are similar but processed only by the destination (or by intermediate nodes if the Routing header is present). Applications use IPV6_DSTOPTS and the same helper functions as for Hop-by-Hop options.

Routing headers allow source routing: the sender specifies a list of intermediate addresses that the packet must visit in order. Applications use IPV6_RTHDR. Helper functions include inet6_rthdr_space(), inet6_rthdr_init(), inet6_rthdr_add() (add an address), inet6_rthdr_reverse() (reverse a list for the reply), and inet6_rthdr_getaddr() (retrieve an address from a header).

Extension headers appear in a defined order: Hop-by-Hop options immediately follow the IPv6 header, then Destination options (if routing is used), then Routing header, then Fragment header (kernel-inserted), then Destination options again (if not already present), then the upper-layer protocol header.
sections.plainLanguage: Extension headers are like extra envelopes inside the packet. Hop-by-Hop options are read by every router. Destination options are read only by the final destination. Routing headers let you specify which routers the packet should visit.

sections.title: IPv4-Mapped IPv6 Addresses and Flow Labels
sections.content:
IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses (written as ::ffff:192.0.2.1) allow IPv6 sockets to communicate with IPv4 hosts. When an IPv6 socket receives a packet from an IPv4 address, it arrives with an IPv4-mapped address. Most socket options and behavior work the same way, but there are some corner cases documented in the RFC.

The IPv6 flow label field (20 bits) is reserved for marking flows that need special treatment (e.g., real-time traffic). This RFC notes it as a future extension; the basic sockets API does not yet standardize how applications set and read flow labels.

The rresvport_af() function allows applications to allocate reserved ports (those below 1024, typically requiring superuser privilege) for both IPv4 and IPv6 connections in a portable way.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv6 can talk to IPv4 if needed using special addresses. Some fields in the header (like flow labels) are reserved for future use.
